title: Friction as Structure: Institutional Governance in the Transition from Reactive to Adaptive Regulation | — A Structural-Analytical Examination
abstract: Short Abstract In the course of the institutional integration of adaptive systems, tensions arise that cannot be described as a deficit of control, but as a structural transition between two governance logics. Reactive governance — developed for stationary objects — operates through ex-post correction, precedent, and formal traceability. Adaptive governance — required for learning systems — demands second-order observation, real-time verification, and structural sensitivity. Friction emerges between these logics. The present work analyzes friction not as a loss to be minimized, but as a structural condition of learning. Drawing on historical parallels (Manhattan Project, financial crisis 2008, platform economy), current institutional movements (chief officer configurations in central banks, supervisory authorities, legislative bodies), and system-theoretical grounding (Luhmann, Meyer/Rowan, Power), a bridging concept is developed: a position that does not reduce reactive and adaptive logic to one another, but maintains them in productive tension. The contribution accomplishes three things. First, a diagnosis of the current governance transition, which has been unfolding since 2024 in European central banks, supervisory authorities, and EU institutions. Second, a theoretical classification that understands the transition not as progress, but as a structural shift — with continuities and ruptures. Third, an analytical instrument that enables institutional decision-makers to locate their own position within the transition and to carry it reflexively. The work is addressed to decision-makers in governance positions, researchers in institutional and regulatory sociology, and reviewers in EU-, ECB-, and BIS-related contexts who are currently operationally engaged with this transition. Purpose of the Paper The paper makes a currently taking-place institutional movement visible as a structural phenomenon that is not yet recognized as such in the institutions involved themselves. Central banks, legislators, supervisory authorities, and compliance structures are moving in parallel toward a new form of institutional governance, without a coordinating event carrying this movement. The parallelism is treated in the ongoing debate as coincidence; the paper reads it as a structural response to a diagnosis that is not formulated in the institutions themselves. The paper provides the institutions involved with an observational point that they cannot occupy from their operative logic. The institution that is currently constructing its institutional response to the integration of adaptive systems cannot test the structural limit of this construction from within the logic in which it is constructing. The paper accomplishes this outside observation — not as critique, but as the provision of a foundation for reflection on which the institution can test its own response, when it takes up the foundation. The paper at the same time introduces into the debate the figure of an institutional function that does not currently exist: a reflexive position that observes the conditions of operative decisions, without entering into the operative decision architecture. This function is set neither as a consultancy offering nor as a theory, but as a structural possibility that becomes necessary under adaptive conditions, and that is currently not provided for in any of the institutional types concerned. The purpose of the paper is thereby not its uptake by the field, not its translation into programs, not its establishment as reference. The purpose is the making available of an observation and a figure for those who can use it in their own institutional constellations. title: SΔφ-60 — Utilitarian Subject-Splitting Index
abstract: SΔφ-60 introduces the Utilitarian Subject-Splitting Index, USSI, within the Sofience-Δφ Formalism. The paper examines whether utilitarian calculation merely evaluates the happiness of already-existing majorities and minorities, or whether such calculation can first produce the operational boundary between majority and minority by redistributing Transition Completion Cost, TCC. The document begins with the Sofience Subject Thought Experiment. A person is imagined as capable of detaching and reattaching any part of the body while the detached parts remain alive, neurologically connected, and physiologically active. Hair, nails, limbs, eyes, tongue, brain, and torso are progressively separated. The experiment asks which part remains closer to the original “I.” SΔφ does not resolve this by locating the subject in a single organ, brain, memory, or bodily part. Instead, it shifts the question from “where is the subject?” to “where does cost return, and which coordinate can edit the path by which cost is attributed?” From this thought experiment, SΔφ-60 defines subjecthood not as a directly measurable essence, but as an operational trace. The subject is not merely the one who thinks, feels, chooses, remembers, or is declared sovereign. The subject is the coordinate that can determine, redirect, authorize, refuse, stabilize, externalize, internalize, or re-enter the path of cost attribution. SΔφ-60 therefore does not claim to measure subjecthood itself. It measures traces of cost-attribution path editing. The paper extends this definition from personal subjecthood to collective and political subjecthood. Majority and minority are not always prior subjects of ethical calculation. They may be produced by repeated cost-attribution patterns. A numerical majority may possess weak operational subjecthood if the TCC required to exercise its formal rights is unbearable. Conversely, a numerical minority may possess strong operational subjecthood if it holds capital, legal authority, technical infrastructure, platform control, administrative access, or discourse power sufficient to redirect cost onto others. SΔφ-60 then introduces the Cost Attribution Path Editing Index, CAPEI, as a supporting index for detecting operational traces of subjecthood. CAPEI measures edit access, edit cost, edit authority, visibility, reversal capacity, re-entry access, burden shift, and closure risk. These dimensions do not identify the subject as a metaphysical essence. They identify whether a coordinate has left measurable traces of editing the path through which costs are distributed. The central index, USSI, evaluates whether a utilitarian diagnosis produces or strengthens subject-splitting. Its dimensions include TCC concentration, externalization asymmetry, re-entry inequality, closure risk, benefit-cost decoupling, CAPEI gap, and numerical-operational subject gap. A high USSI does not automatically refute utilitarianism. It indicates that a utilitarian calculation may be generating or reinforcing the very majority/minority boundary it claims merely to evaluate. The paper also applies this framework to democratic sovereignty. Democratic states may declare that the people are sovereign, yet operational subjecthood depends on whether citizens can actually edit the paths through which costs are attributed. A right that cannot be exercised without unbearable TCC is formally present but operationally weak. SΔφ-60 therefore separates nominal sovereignty from operational subjecthood. Finally, SΔφ-60 distinguishes types of civic organization. The existence of civic organizations does not by itself prove that civil society is operational. Civic organizations may enable genuine re-entry, function as nominal or state-aligned civic interfaces, perform diagnostic theater, become captured by power, or mobilize citizens without granting real editing authority. The document therefore treats civil society not as a label, but as a question of whether cost-bearing groups can re-enter institutional editing paths at bearable TCC. SΔφ-60 incorporates the measurement safeguards established in SΔφ-56 v1.1. Every USSI or CAPEI report should include Unmeasured Remainder, Observer Position, Exclusion Register, Measurement-Induced Cost, and Revision Path. Without such safeguards, a subject-splitting score may itself become another instrument of subject-splitting.

title: Quality Engineering for Intelligence (Verification Intelligence series, Paper 3 of 12)
abstract: The previous papers in this series established two propositions. The first is that verification — the capacity to determine whether intelligence corresponds to reality — is becoming the scarce resource of the intelligence age. The second is that intelligence systems operating without adequate verification diverge from reality through recursive feedback, becoming more internally coherent and more externally wrong with each cycle. This paper argues that the challenge is not new. The discipline of quality engineering confronted and substantially solved a structurally identical problem over the course of the twentieth century: the challenge of producing reliable outputs from complex processes operating under uncertainty. The solutions developed by Deming, Juran, Shewhart, Toyota, and the broader quality movement share a foundational insight: reliability does not emerge as a by-product of capability. It must be engineered. Deming provided the philosophical foundation: quality is a systemic property that cannot be inspected into a product after production. Juran provided the operational framework: quality must be planned, controlled, and improved as a management discipline, with measurable costs and structured processes. Together, they demonstrated that the relationship between a process and reality must be architecturally maintained — not assumed, hoped for, or retroactively verified. Artificial intelligence now faces the same transition. The industry has invested enormously in capability. It has invested comparatively little in the systematic verification architectures that would determine whether those capabilities produce reliable outcomes in practice. The quality engineering tradition offers both the diagnosis and the architectural precedent for what must be built. ---

title: Mitigating Climate Change Risks by Adopting Emerging Technologies: A Contextual Comparative Exploration of Fast Fashion Supply Chains
abstract: Abstract Empirical research suggests that the fast fashion (FF) industry is a major contributor to global climate change. Fast-fashion supply chains (FFSCs) are inherently complex due to the multiplicity of processes, locations, and stakeholders involved. This research explores the key climate change risks, response strategies, and application of emerging technologies in the comparative context of developing and developed countries. Institutional theory was used as a theoretical lens, and the research data were collected by using expert interviews from industry experts in Pakistan and the UK. The analysis shows numerous climate change risks posed by FFSC at multiple tiers, ranging from raw materials to the retailing of products. The FF industry in Pakistan is more focused on meeting the needs of UK fashion brands by adopting global frameworks to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions, including using sustainable materials and adopting changes according to the environmental standards and renewable energy due to coercive, normative, and mimetic pressures. In contrast, coercive and mimetic pressures forcing UK fashion companies to address regulatory and economic challenges and deal with persistent organisational and cultural issues including fast-changing customer requirements. To mitigate climate change risks, companies in both contexts are adopting emerging technologies such as AI-based analytics, internet of things, automation, blockchain and digital traceability-based solutions, and 3D printing. However, they face challenges such as high initial costs, human capital gaps, and data integration issues. To mitigate these challenges, companies in both contexts are adopting strategies such as technology–business alignment, collaboration with technology partners and multiple stakeholders, pilot testing of new technologies, cultural transformation, and structural changes.

title: Decoding technology transition process through consumer behavior: experience from China’s electric vehicle evolution
abstract: The competition between electric vehicles (EVs) and internal combustion engine vehicles is fundamentally shaped by how heterogeneous consumers respond to technological and market change. This study develops a decision-based framework that links micro-level adoption behavior with macro-level fleet dynamics. Using China as the core case, we identify three consumer segments: new, replacement, and renewal buyers, and show that they react differently to purchase cost, usability, and charging conditions. Embedding these segments in a dynamic simulation suggests a conditional phased transition under the baseline scenario: EV stock may overtake ICEVs around 2030, and the expansion of the secondhand EV market after 2035 could reshape buyer composition and strengthen the role of replacement demand. A cross-national comparison of 51 countries further shows that economic development stages and institutional capacity mediate how these behavioral logics translate into market outcomes, from infrastructure and affordability constraints in emerging EV markets to norm-driven, autonomous adoption in advanced EV markets. The findings highlight that EV transitions are driven by the interaction between consumer heterogeneity and market development, providing a behavioral basis for stage-specific policies and infrastructure strategies worldwide.

title: Does sleep matter for recovery after stroke? Functional severity shapes the association between sleep and functional outcome during inpatient stroke rehabilitation
abstract: Abstract Background Sleep disturbances are common after stroke and have been associated with rehabilitation outcomes. The clinical meaning of post-stroke sleep duration remains unclear, as longer sleep may be associated with different clinical and functional states, including greater disability. This exploratory study investigated the relationship between sleep and functional outcome during stroke rehabilitation, and the moderating role of baseline functional status. Methods Twenty-nine patients with stroke underwent a 10-day longitudinal monitoring protocol during rehabilitation. Functional independence and motor performance were assessed at the beginning (T0) and the end (T1) of the observation period using the Barthel Index, 10-Meter Walk Test, and 9-Hole Peg Test. Sleep was assessed throughout the monitoring period using sleep diaries, and actigraphy . Results Functional independence improved from T0 to T1, whereas motor performance did not significantly change. In unadjusted analyses, longer actigraphy-derived total sleep time and longer self-reported total time in bed were correlated with lower Barthel Index scores at T1. Moderation analyses adjusted for prior rehabilitation days showed that longer total sleep time was positively associated with Barthel Index at T1 only in patients with higher baseline independence, while longer time in bed was positively associated at average and higher baseline levels. Conclusions The associations between sleep duration or time in bed and later post-rehabilitation functional independence vary according to baseline functional status. Given the small sample size and observational design, these findings should be interpreted cautiously and considered preliminary and hypothesis-generating.

title: President’s Column: Make the Most of ATCE 2026: A Strategic Investment in Your Career and Organization
abstract: _ October is an exciting time for SPE members around the world because it means the Annual Technical Conference and Exhibition (ATCE) is nearly here. title: Zyfralon Issuance Standard (ZIS): A Public Qualification Thesis for Institutional Readiness, Admission, and Continuing Eligibility of Public-Facing Commercial Enterprises
abstract: This paper develops the public thesis for the Zyfralon Issuance Standard (ZIS), a proposed framework for qualification, admission readiness, and continuing eligibility of Public-Facing Commercial Enterprises (PFCEs). It argues that access to a specialized market should depend on evidence, rights, governance, disclosure, and institutional readiness rather than fame, momentum, or audience size alone. Drawing on exchange practice, peer-reviewed IPO and certification research, creator-economy scholarship, World Federation of Exchanges research, securities-law doctrine, and relevant case law, the paper explains why qualification should operate upstream of price discovery while remaining separate from valuation, security design, regulatory authorization, venue authorization, and investment merit. The paper distinguishes PFCE classification, ZIS qualification, ZEVS enterprise evaluation, ZES instrument design, lawful venue authorization, and market price formation as separate institutional functions. It also explains the importance of legal-issuer accountability, rights control, financial integrity, governance, disclosure capability, evidence integrity, continuity, suitability, continuing eligibility, procedural fairness, human accountability, and calibrated market-entry standards. The public paper intentionally withholds exact thresholds, category floors, gate mechanics, routing logic, anti-gaming controls, surveillance methods, internal reviewer instructions, implementation code, and other restricted operating specifications.

title: Nuclear norm regularized estimation of panel regression models
abstract: In this paper we investigate panel regression models with interactive fixed effects. We propose two new estimation methods that are based on minimizing convex objective functions. The first method minimizes the sum of squared residuals with a nuclear (trace) norm regularization. The second method minimizes the nuclear norm of the residuals. We establish the consistency of the two resulting estimators. Those estimators have a very important computational advantage compared to the existing least squares (LS) estimator, in that they are defined as minimizers of a convex objective function. In addition, the nuclear norm penalization helps to resolve a potential identification problem for interactive fixed effect models, in particular when the regressors are low-rank and the number of the factors is unknown. We also show how to construct estimators that are asymptotically equivalent to the least squares (LS) estimator in Bai(2009) and Moo(2017) by using our nuclear norm regularized or minimized estimators as initial values for a finite number of LS minimizing iteration steps. This iteration avoids any non-convex minimization, while the original LS estimation problem is generally non-convex, and can have multiple local minima.

title: The Theory of Data
abstract: A value becomes data only when it is bound to something it is about. The Theory of Data (ToD) develops a compact ontology for governed analytical objects. A universe establishes a governed root-point domain under an explicit existence law. An anchor is a governed partition of that universe. A measure family supplies analytical identity and family law. A measure is one family at one anchor, written F@A. Version 6.1 makes the identity criterion operationally explicit. Family identity is determined ex ante from a governed semantic signature, independently of agreement or disagreement among computed outputs. An implementation may assign an opaque immutable family_id to that signature; canonical names remain governed resolvable handles. Identity is therefore an input to a consistency test, never an inference from its result. The revision separates four locations for governance information: family identity, edge validity, certificate/materialization, and metadata. Meaning-bearing participation, multiplicity, unit, regime, and related semantics belong to family identity when they change the quantity or its declared family law. Edge predicates determine whether a particular derivation faithfully realizes that identity. Exactness, approximation, retained capability, and evidence grade belong to the certificate/materialization layer when the semantic target is unchanged. Inside a measure family, the central coherence theorem uses commutative-monoid sufficient state. The underlying algebra is standard; ToD's contribution is architectural: the state law is attached to family identity and edge contracts so that staging equivalence becomes a governed property. Version 6.1 adds a state-law taxonomy for commutative, order-sensitive, ordered/stateful, and non-decomposable cases. Partition anchors remain foundational. Many-to-many membership, overlapping cohorts, and fractional allocations are handled through governed assignment, allocation, expansion, or derived membership universes while partition geometry remains intact. Multi-parent lineage is illustrated with Average Order Value. A minimal conformance appendix shows how universes, anchors, families, edges, certificates, immutable IDs, and semantic signatures can be declared while keeping institutional authority outside the ontology. The claim remains narrow. ToD governs analytical identity, derivability, consistency, lineage, and materialized capability under declared premises. Empirical truth and statistical warrant require their own evidential grounds.

title: Does Time Need Me, or Do I Need Time?
abstract: This essay develops a metaphysical account of time in which the present (the Now) is treated as an invariant condition of actualization rather than a moving moment within a temporal sequence. Against the common assumption that time flows and the present passes, the argument proposes that the Now is a singular, non-extended point at which all events are continuously actualized. What is experienced as temporal flow is not the movement of the Now itself but the succession of events occurring within it. Time, in this framework, is not a substance but a dependent condition, arising only where change occurs within space and matter. The Now, as the condition of all actualization, cannot sustain itself and therefore points to a non-temporal ground that holds it open. This leads to a philosophical account of divine presence understood not as a being within time, but as the sustaining source of the Now itself. The essay further argues that the singularity of the Now implies the singularity of the self: identity is constituted not by possible alternatives but by actualization within the one shared present. The resulting framework—referred to as a lemniscatic topology of time—offers a unified account of temporality, agency, and metaphysical grounding.

title: Green consumer behavior in e-commerce: The mediating role of digital engagement and the moderating effects of literacy and environmental knowledge
abstract: This study aims to identify the factors influencing digital engagement behavior and online shopping intention in the context of green e-commerce. Extending prior studies that have often examined green consumption, mobile shopping experience, and platform sustainability as separate research streams, this study develops an integrated model explaining how value-related, brand-related, experience-related, and platform-related factors jointly shape green e-commerce behavior through digital engagement. Data were collected from consumers in Vietnam through a quantitative survey and analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The results show that green perceived value, eco-brand credibility, mobile shopping experience, and platform sustainability features positively influence digital engagement behavior and online shopping intention. Furthermore, digital engagement behavior plays an important mediating role, clarifying the behavioral mechanism through which consumers move from green awareness and digital platform experience to online shopping intention. Meanwhile, digital literacy and environmental knowledge significantly strengthen the effect of digital engagement behavior on online shopping intention, demonstrating the important role of these competencies in sustainable consumption. By integrating green value perception, eco-brand credibility, mobile shopping experience, platform sustainability features, digital engagement, and consumer competencies into a single explanatory framework, this study offers novel evidence on green e-commerce behavior in an emerging economy context. This study contributes to expanding the understanding of green consumer behavior on digital platforms and proposes strategic directions for e-commerce businesses seeking to promote sustainable online consumption.

title: Effect on Decision Making Processes of Pythagorean Fuzzy Set
abstract: Pythagorean Fuzzy Set concept is a more flexible approach that encompasses fuzzy sets and intuitionistic fuzzy sets in the uncertainty modeling process. The concept offers a new approach for jointly evaluating membership and non-membership degrees. This approach allows decision makers to express uncertainty over a wider range. Therefore, Pythagorean fuzzy sets offer higher representational power than intuitionistic fuzzy sets and are particularly effective in solving complex problems such as multi-criteria decision making, risk analysis, expert systems. Decision making is an approach that aims to systematically analyze decision problems that consider multiple criteria. This method allows the decision maker to evaluate both qualitative and quantitative factors to make the most appropriate choice among alternatives. Among the most commonly used methods, AHP, TOPSIS and PROMETHEE are prominent, aiming to determine the relative advantages of alternatives under different assumptions. Today, fuzzy logic and its extended forms, intuitionistic and pythagorean fuzzy approaches, are frequently integrated into decision making processes to reduce the influence of uncertainty, expert judgment, and subjective assessments. This allows decision models to more effectively represent the complex and uncertain situations encountered in real life problems. This study presents an example of the impact of pythagorean fuzzy sets on decision-making processes.

title: From “curse” to “gospel”: how can industrial relocation lead cities to cross the resource dependence gap
abstract: Industrial relocation offers a novel solution to help mitigate the “resource curse” by reducing dependence on natural resources and fostering diversified economic systems, thereby optimizing the industrial structure. This paper explores the mechanism and economic consequences of industrial relocation’s dependence on the host country’s resources, focusing on the National Industrial Relocation Demonstration Zones (NIRDZ). Theoretical analysis using urban panel statistics from 2006 to 2022 investigates the relationship between industrial relocation and the host’s resource dependence through a multi-period Difference-in-Differences. The heterogeneity of the policy effect is analyzed from a three-dimensional urban attribute perspective encompassing “location-feature-scale.” The results indicate that: (1) Industrial relocation can significantly restrain resource dependence and thereby help alleviate the “resource curse,” a conclusion that remains valid following multiple robustness tests. (2) Industrial relocation mainly inhibits urban resource dependence by reducing energy consumption, increasing the level of foreign investment, and enhancing technological innovation. (3) Heterogeneity analysis demonstrates that the NIRDZ policy exerts a more pronounced inhibitory effect on resource dependence in central cities, non-provincial-capital cities, and cities with smaller populations. Unlike the cracking strategy proposed by most previous studies on resource management, this paper reveals that central cities can provide a viable pathway to alleviating the “resource curse” by developing industries in the eastern region. This not only establishes a foundation for decision-making regarding the green transformation and sustainable development of resource-rich cities but also contributes to new empirical evidence to the “resource curse” governance literature.
venue: Humanities and Social Sciences Communications

title: Framework for user-centred design and pre-occupancy design evaluation of higher education buildings
abstract: Purpose Higher education (HE) buildings often exhibit persistent performance gaps that compromise user comfort, health and satisfaction. These adverse outcomes are frequently linked to inadequate end-user engagement in the design phase. This study develops and validates a holistic framework for end-user engagement that systematically integrates user inputs throughout the design process to enable user-centred design and pre-occupancy evaluation, proactively mitigating performance gaps. Design/methodology/approach The framework was formulated through an integrative review and idea mapping from three knowledge areas: user engagement theories, functional performance specification and design elements. The framework was validated through 70 structured interviews: 35 with end-users, 17 with HE building professionals, and 18 with industry architects. Quantitative data were analysed using descriptive statistics, Kruskal–Wallis and Dunn tests. Qualitative insights were examined through content analysis. Findings The study presents a novel framework featuring a process-flow model and modules for user-requirements acquisition and design evaluation to engage end-users throughout HE building design. The framework’s overall effectiveness for end-user involvement across pre-design, schematic and detailed design was rated 8.4 out of 10. Study participants identified many benefits of the framework, including comprehensiveness, facilitation of end-user engagement across all design stages, adaptability, quantifiable scoring, stimulation of user reflection, ease of distribution and robustness. Originality/value The systemised framework addresses longstanding barriers to end-user engagement in HE building design. Its modular and traceable structure enables those with limited experience to implement structured engagement practices. By facilitating early, evidence-based user input, the framework promotes people-centred design, minimises post-occupancy modifications and enhances building performance and user satisfaction.

title: Zyfralon Enterprise Security (ZES): A Public Principles Thesis for a Participation-Only Market Instrument
abstract: This paper establishes the public principles of the proposed Zyfralon Enterprise Security (ZES), the participation-only instrument within the Zyfralon architecture. ZES is designed to permit lawful market participation in relation to an admitted Public-Facing Commercial Enterprise without silently converting that participation into ordinary equity, ownership of an enterprise or public identity, a claim on issuer revenue, intellectual-property or name-image-likeness rights, governance control, or a guaranteed economic return. The paper defines the participation-only boundary; distinguishes the PFCE, legal issuer, instrument, analytical assessment, market venue, and market price; and explains ZES’s relationship to PFCE classification, ZIS qualification, ZEVS evaluation, lawful issuance, disclosure, recordkeeping, transfer, lifecycle governance, and market integrity. It emphasizes that rights arise only from complete governing terms and applicable law, that PFCE classification, ZIS qualification, and ZEVS evaluation do not themselves authorize issuance, and that ZEVS output is not market price. The public paper intentionally excludes proprietary contractual mechanics, formulas, thresholds, surveillance logic, control logic, routing, system mappings, and implementation specifications.

title: Revealing graph bandits for maximizing local influence
abstract: We study a graph bandit setting where the objective of the learner is to detect the most influential node of a graph by requesting as little information from the graph as possible. One of the relevant applications for this setting is marketing in social networks, where the marketer aims at finding and taking advantage of the most influential customers. The existing approaches for bandit problems on graphs require either partial or complete knowledge of the graph. In this paper, we do not assume any knowledge of the graph, but we consider a setting where it can be gradually discovered in a sequential and active way. At each round, the learner chooses a node of the graph and the only information it receives is a stochastic set of the nodes that the chosen node is currently influencing. To address this setting, we propose BARE, a bandit strategy for which we prove a regret guarantee that scales with the detectable dimension, a problem dependent quantity that is often much smaller than the number of nodes.

title: The Shape of the Tax: Transaction Shifting at New York City's 2019 Transfer-Tax Notches and the Mortgage Recording Tax
abstract: New York's 2019 budget created seven buyer-paid transfer-tax notches on one date, from USD 2 million to USD 25 million, and left the USD 1 million mansion-tax notch unchanged. The paper compares sale prices at the same thresholds before and after the reform, with the USD 1 million threshold as a control. At each new threshold with enough sales to measure, sales moved to just below it. The shift is larger than at any of sixteen never-taxed round prices below USD 6 million, and a year-by-year event study shows it starting with the reform. It appears in houses and condominiums and does not come from foreclosure transfers. The shift remains evident without company sellers; among company-seller sales, a proxy that includes sponsor sales whose prices developers set in advance, it is clear only at USD 3 million. At USD 2 million and USD 3 million, the range of prices emptied above the threshold is two to three times as wide as the tax jump. The response does not grow in proportion to the buyer's rate increase: the sampling bootstrap rejects proportionality, and comparisons with placebo noise point the same way more weakly. Equal responses are not established either. If the extra sales below each threshold came from above it, the avoided tax is USD 2–3 million a year, 2–3% of the revenue the reform's schedule implies between USD 2 million and USD 6 million. The paper then applies these results to New York City's mortgage recording tax, which charges borrowers 1.80–1.925% of the loan and charges a purchase without a mortgage nothing. Applied to the recorded principal of 172,725 observed loans, the schedule implies a gross charge that averages 1.41% of price for houses and 1.28% for condominiums, before credits, exemptions and consolidation adjustments. With transactions held fixed, the gross schedule-implied charge is about USD 244 million a year on residential purchase money between USD 300,000 and USD 6 million in four boroughs, and the paper costs continuous schedules that would raise the same static amount. The paper identifies neither economic incidence nor an optimal tax. Version 2.6 makes six wording changes after a final cross-check, with no change to any estimate. The recording-tax figures are labelled as gross schedule-implied charges. The financing flag is described as a matched mortgage instrument. Company-seller groups replace the claim that most of the response comes from resales. The avoided-tax figure is conditional on relocation across thresholds. Inference wording is made descriptive where the tests do not support more. Replication package version 1.9 reproduces this version. Version 2.5 corrected the placebo inference. Size-matched placebo draws are now taken with replacement; version 2.4 drew them without replacement, so they varied less than repeated samples would. The main results are unchanged. Placebo ranks and tail shares are now described as reference comparisons, not exact tests. The recording-tax table's condominium row now uses the 47,702 loans of the public linked dataset, with the same statistics as before, so the replication package reproduces it. Replication package version 1.8 reproduced it. See revision_notes.md for details.

title: What Is the Past? On Closed Confluence, Condensation, and the Being of What Has Been
abstract: This essay asks what the past actually is within the Gaitan Topology. Building on When Is the Present? and Whose Condensation Am I?, it argues that the past is not a place behind the Now, nor an archive of vanished events, but a confluence whose reception has completed. What has been received is not erased when the confluence closes; it is condensed into the constitution of what is now actual, persisting as trace and structural inertia. The essay distinguishes the past from memory, showing that memory is a selective and fallible reconstruction of a constitution that remains ontologically complete. It also distinguishes completed actuality, present constitution, and memory as three registers of temporal inheritance. Finally, the essay examines Isaiah’s command concerning the former things, the newness of mercy, and the ground that sustains the present. The resulting definition is concise: the past is closed confluence—a completed reception that is no longer open, yet remains constitutive of what is now.

title: The Verification Substrate (Verification Intelligence series, Paper 5 of 12)
abstract: The previous paper proposed a redefinition of intelligence: not the capacity to generate but the capacity to reduce uncertainty about reality. This paper addresses the architectural question that follows: given that redefinition, what does a system designed around verification actually look like? Six principles — derived by direct architectural correspondence with the scientific method — define what a verification-first system requires: claims as the atomic unit, confidence decoupled from verification status, positions as emergent evidence-dependent structures, adversarial audit as a standing function, multi-layer verification with independent operation, and a persistent substrate with accumulating verification. The paper introduces Recursive General Intelligence (RGI) to describe systems implementing these principles — distinguished from AGI by what each optimises for. AGI optimises for breadth of capability. RGI optimises for depth and reliability of understanding, measured through the density and verification status of its knowledge substrate. The distinction produces fundamentally different systems. A generation-first system delivers the same reliability on day one thousand as on day one. A verification-first system compounds. ---

title: How "Buy Now, Pay Later" Changes the Psychology of Spending" A Conceptual/Comparative Analysis of BNPL and the Traditional Credit Card
abstract: Abstract Buy now, pay later (BNPL) is typically described as either a harmless budgeting tool or a repackaged form of consumer debt. Neither framing explains why a product that charges no interest and divides a purchase into four small instalments has produced spending increases, delinquency patterns, nor was self-reported regret that closely resemble the credit card habits it intended to replace. This paper argues that BNPL and credit cards likely do not operate through the same psychological mechanism at different intensities, but through structurally different mechanisms that converge on similar financial harm. Drawing on Federal Reserve, CFPB, Central Bank of Ireland, and peer-reviewed data, the paper develops two original analytical tools: a taxonomy that separates six frequently conflated “BNPL effect” statistics according to what each actually measures and the strength of evidence behind it, and a framework termed the Debt Visibility Paradox, which decomposes “invisible debt” into four separately testable constructs — borrower recall, credit-bureau visibility, statement visibility, and cash-flow burden — rather than treating it as a single impression. The working conclusion is that BNPL may not so much reduce the pain of paying as redistribute it into units too small for existing disclosure rules to register.

title: Institute-created electronic flashcards, associated development effort, and exam performance in pharmacology education in human medicine
abstract: Abstract Electronic flashcards are popular among medical students, although their real-world effectiveness, and staff resources required to develop tailored decks, is not well understood. The Institute of Experimental and Clinical Pharmacology, Toxicology and Pharmacology of Natural Products at the Ulm University Medical Center, Germany, created 1007 flashcards on 228 drugs aligned to the local and national curriculum using the Anki flashcard software. The time needed for card development was documented. Medical students participated in an observational study over four semesters and were encouraged to use the cards alongside established study materials for exam preparation in clinical pharmacology. Exams concluded either a lecture-based course focusing on declarative knowledge, or concluded a seminar-based course focusing on case-based application. A survey assessed usage patterns and helpfulness of flashcards and other study materials, demographics, and self-rated general academic performance. Pseudonymous codes linked survey responses to individual exam scores. Flashcard use was reported by 38.4% of participants overall, with higher use when preparing for lecture-based exams than for seminar-based exams. In total, 83.3% of users considered the cards helpful. Participants with lower self-rated general academic performance were more likely to use flashcards. Flashcard users scored lower in the exam than non-users, but this association was no longer significant after adjusting for self-rated general academic performance. Flashcard development took on average 7 min per card. These findings suggest that academically weaker students, and students preparing for exams testing declarative knowledge, may prefer flashcards. Given the substantial staff time required, and the lacking benefit of our flashcard-decks, the decision to tailor curriculum-aligned flashcards should be made cautiously.

title: Hitting Rewind: The Supreme Court of Pennsylvania in Trust Under Agreement of Taylor Signals a Move Away from Modern Developments of Trust Law by Requiring More Stringent Standards for Corporate Trustee Removal
abstract: This Casebrief examines the Supreme Court of Pennsylvania’s decision in Trust Under Agreement of Taylor and argues that the court narrowly limited beneficiaries’ ability to remove corporate trustees by holding that trustee removal must proceed exclusively under Section 7766 of the Uniform Trust Act. The Casebrief contends that the decision reinforces traditional deference to settlor intent while highlighting continuing concerns about the power imbalance between corporate trustees and beneficiaries.[This abstract was written by Microsoft Copilot, a generative artificial intelligence.]

title: Zyfralon Enterprise Valuation System (ZEVS): The Standardized Analytical Framework Developed for Public-Facing Commercial Enterprises (PFCEs)
abstract: The Public-Facing Commercial Enterprise (PFCE) thesis identifies an institutional category of commercially operated enterprises whose economic activity is materially connected to a recognizable public identity, intellectual-property portfolio, constituency, or other public-facing commercial relationship, and whose enterprise condition can be examined through documented rights, financial activity, contracts, operations, governance, and risk. Defining that category creates a second problem: how should enterprises with materially different commercial forms be evaluated through a common analytical language without reducing popularity to value or forcing every PFCE into the same monetary valuation model? The Zyfralon Enterprise Valuation System (ZEVS) was developed specifically for that PFCE problem. ZEVS is a standardized enterprise-evaluation framework that organizes verified PFCE evidence across eight public analytical domains: Financial Performance; Enterprise Operations; Public Constituency Strength; Brand Equity; Intellectual Property; Commercial Contracts; Growth & Momentum; and Enterprise Risk Strength. Its output is an analytical enterprise profile, not a market price, target price, credit rating, or investment recommendation. This paper argues that PFCEs sharpen a recurring institutional problem: commercially meaningful value can be distributed across financial, rights-based, contractual, operational, constituency, brand, and risk evidence that conventional reporting and specialized valuation disciplines often examine separately. Conventional valuation remains indispensable. ZEVS contributes an upstream layer: it makes the PFCE more analytically legible before purpose-specific monetary valuation and market price compress the enterprise into a monetary conclusion

title: A Survey on Human–AI Collaboration with Large Foundation Models
abstract: As the capabilities of artificial intelligence (AI) continue to expand rapidly, Human–AI (HAI) Collaboration, combining human intellect and AI systems, has become pivotal for advancing problem-solving and decision-making processes. The advent of Large Foundation Models (LFMs) has greatly expanded its potential, offering unprecedented capabilities by leveraging vast amounts of data to understand and predict complex patterns. At the same time, realizing this potential responsibly requires addressing persistent challenges related to safety, fairness, and control. This article reviews the crucial integration of LFMs with HAI, highlighting both opportunities and risks. We structure our analysis around human-guided model development, collaborative design principles, ethical and governance frameworks, and applications in high-stakes domains. Our review shows that successful HAI systems are not the automatic result of stronger models but the product of careful, human-centered design. By identifying key open challenges, this survey aims to give insight into current and future research that turns the raw power of LFMs into partnerships that are reliable, trustworthy, and beneficial to society.
venue: ACM Transactions on Intelligent Systems and Technology

title: A Temporary VAT Cut as Unconventional Fiscal Policy
abstract: Abstract We exploit Germany’s temporary three-percentage-point value-added tax (VAT) cut in the second half of 2020 to study the spending response to unconventional fiscal policy. We use survey and scanner data on household consumption expenditures and their perceived pass-through of the tax change into prices, and a HANK model to quantify the effects of this VAT policy. The survey and scanner data show that the temporary VAT reduction led to a relative increase in durable and, to a lesser extent, semi-durable spending for individuals with high perceived pass-through. According to the HANK model, the VAT policy increased total aggregate consumption spending by 4.4% on impact.

title: The Trust Layer (Verification Intelligence series, Paper 7 of 12)
abstract: Each major civilisational infrastructure layer has enabled the next. Communication infrastructure created the telephone network and the internet. Information infrastructure created search and the indexed web. Computational infrastructure created cloud computing and on-demand processing. Intelligence infrastructure — artificial intelligence — is being built now. This paper argues that the current trajectory is constructing the intelligence layer without the layer that must sit above it: verification. And that verification, operating at scale over time, produces something more valuable than intelligence alone: trust. *The Trust Layer is the civilisational infrastructure that converts verified intelligence into justified confidence — the persistent, accumulating, domain-independent substrate against which intelligence outputs are tested and through which systems earn the right to operate autonomously. It is to the intelligence age what the scientific method is to the knowledge age: the mechanism by which claims are tested against reality, and the infrastructure without which capability alone cannot produce reliability. Trust, as defined in this paper, is not a feeling, a marketing claim, or a decision to believe. It is justified confidence that a system's outputs have been verified against reality — a structural property of systems with demonstrated track records, not a psychological property of their users. As AI systems become increasingly autonomous — taking actions, managing resources, and making decisions without human oversight at every step — the operative question shifts from "is this specific output correct?" to "can this system be trusted?" That question cannot be answered without verification infrastructure, for the same reason that commerce cannot function without payment infrastructure and science cannot function without the scientific method. The idea that AI systems require verification is not new. Constitutional AI, formal verification methods, the EU AI Act's risk-based assessment framework, and dedicated verification institutions such as AVERI all reflect growing recognition that verification must be addressed. What remains largely unbuilt is verification as infrastructure* — not as a feature of individual systems or a requirement imposed by regulation, but as a shared, persistent, accumulating layer upon which the entire intelligence economy can operate. This paper proposes that verification is the missing civilisational infrastructure layer, that trust is what emerges when verification operates at scale, and that the organisations and systems that build verification infrastructure will hold structural advantages that capability improvements alone cannot replicate. This is the seventh paper in a series that has traced the path from the Verification Deficit (Paper 1) through the Recursive Hallucination Principle (Paper 2), Quality Engineering for Intelligence (Paper 3), Verification Intelligence as the stabilising function that maintains intelligence's relationship with reality (Paper 4), the architectural principles for verification-first systems in The Verification Substrate (Paper 5), and the accumulation of Machine Wisdom through verified experience (Paper 6) to arrive at its destination: trust as the defining infrastructure of the intelligence age. ---

title: From Innovation to Enterprise: the Role of Patent Law in Promoting Entrepreneurship and Start-Ups in India
abstract: AbstractInnovation drives entrepreneurship, technological progress and economic growth. For technology-based start-ups, patent protection helps transform innovative ideas into viable businesses by safeguarding inventions and facilitating investment, licensing, technology transfer and market expansion. This paper examines how patent law supports entrepreneurship and start-ups in India, focusing on the Patents Act, 1970, National IPR Policy, 2016, Start-up India and SIPP. It highlights challenges such as costs, limited awareness, procedural complexities and commercialization gaps. The study concludes that patents can promote innovation and competitiveness, but their success depends on broader support through finance, incubation, technology transfer and effective enforcement.

title: Customer Satisfaction In Public Sector Banks: Balancing The Digital Push And The Human Touch In India
abstract: Abstract The Indian banking sector has shifted dramatically from manual ledgers to advanced digital platforms. Public Sector Banks (PSBs), the backbone of the country’s financial system, have led this charge. Yet, despite heavy tech investments, customer satisfaction remains a pressing concern. This study explores the link between service quality, digital banking experience, and customer satisfaction in PSBs. Using a mixed-methods approach, we gathered data from 428 customers across urban and semi-urban areas in Karnataka, Maharashtra, and Tamil Nadu. Blending the SERVQUAL model with digital experience parameters, the findings show that while digital infrastructure has improved, the human element still dictates overall satisfaction. Customers like digital convenience but feel frustrated by poor grievance redressal and the digital divide affecting senior citizens. The study suggests a balanced "phygital" approach—using technology for efficiency while preserving the personal trust that remains a PSB's core strength.

title: A Wrinkle in Title VII: Rigid Evidentiary Requirements and Inadequate Causation Tests Trammel Women's Sex-Plus-Age Claims
abstract: This Comment examines the Tenth Circuit’s decision in Frappied v. Affinity Gaming Black Hawk, LLC and argues that, although the court recognized sex-plus-age claims under Title VII, older women remain disadvantaged by rigid comparator requirements and causation standards. The Comment contends that these doctrines make it difficult for women to prove discrimination based on the intersection of sex and age, particularly in appearance-driven industries where older male comparators are often unavailable. It concludes that the current framework limits the practical value of sex-plus-age claims and leaves many older women without an effective remedy for workplace discrimination.[This abstract was written by Microsoft Copilot, a generative artificial intelligence.]

title: Executable Capability Percolation Theory
abstract: Executable Capability Percolation Theory (ECPT) is a mathematical framework for studying how execution-available capability packets can accumulate, combine, and propagate through constrained directed hypergraphs. The theory models ASI-proxy phase approach as a typed phase-control problem rather than as an absolute claim about artificial superintelligence. It separates settled, provisional, and speculative target claims, and represents capability growth through stochastic relaxation quotients, global Gibbs activation, speculative RAF-like closure, liquidity-debt settlement, reachable-mass recursion, and intervention-identified mean-field envelopes. This version emphasizes operability and machine readability. It introduces constructed path-law response policies, log-linked generator identification, finite-sample quotient certification, self-normalized risk margins, AND-support activation thresholds, and protocol-relative checker soundness. The TeX source also embeds a machine-readable manifest, claim registry, citation metadata, CodeMeta JSON-LD, and BibTeX mirror, making the artifact suitable for reproducible mathematical review and metadata indexing.

title: Associations of Physical Activity and Psychological Resilience with Non-Suicidal Self-Injury Among Chinese Adolescents: A Combined Variable- and Person-Centered Approach
abstract: Non-suicidal self-injury (NSSI) among adolescents is an important public health concern. This study examined the associations among physical activity (PA), psychological resilience (PR), and NSSI among 2257 junior high school students aged 12-17 years in central China. Using both variable-centered and person-centered approaches, the study found that higher PA and higher PR were related to lower NSSI. PR also partly accounted for the association between PA and NSSI, suggesting that resilience may be one pathway linking physical activity to reduced self-injury risk. Latent profile analysis identified three PA-PR profiles: low, moderate, and high. Adolescents in the low PA-PR profile reported the highest NSSI risk, whereas those in the high PA-PR profile reported the lowest risk. These findings suggest that interventions promoting PA and resilience may help reduce adolescent NSSI risk.

title: Libraries within the Library: The Origins of the British Library’s Printed Collections
abstract: Dispersed along the shelves of the British Library today are many volumes that once stood side by side in private libraries. These essays explore some of the most important printed collections which were brought together to form the British Museum Library and cast new light on the individuals whose personal interests and taste they reflect.

title: A Comparative Study on Consumer Preferences and Buying Patterns between Organized and Unorganized Retail Formats in Maharashtra
abstract: Abstract Indian economy has grown rapidly in the last two decades, as a result of change in the business environment and thereby attracted massive investment from domestic and foreign players. This study is an effort to understand the revolution which has taken place in the Indian retail industry. Moreover, with the help of this study the researcher has made an attempt to analyze the shopping behaviour of consumer and try to assess consumer's perception with respect to organized retailer. In order to analyze the consumer's perception a survey has been conducted in Mumbai city and suburbs and based on the survey findings has been drawn by the researcher. The findings are based on the structured questionnaire collected from 100 respondents and the data has been collected through convenience sampling method. Organized retailer's popularity among the consumers is growing and thereby favouring the Mall culture which is quite prevalent in the Western Countries. Specially, youth prefer to shop more at modern retail formats as compared to consumer of adult and mature age groups. Moreover the research also highlight that Indian consumers are price sensitive also.

title: Beyond Magic and Godlike Authority Clarke's Third Law, Shermer's Last Law, and the Epistemology of AGI and SGI
abstract: Clarke’s Third Law and Shermer’s Last Law motivate a distinction between extraordinarycapability, accessible evidence, and attributed authority. We develop this distinction for artificialgeneral intelligence and superhuman general intelligence, including the conditional possibilitythat an AI invents useful mathematical metalanguages and teaches human-accessible fragments.Resource-bounded experiments, selected-demonstration models, checked proof transport, and ataught-observer theorem connect semantic learning to scoped decision risk. Public 2026 incidentdisclosures motivate a further distinction: understanding and final approval do not control effectsalready produced during loading, translation, evidence acquisition, memory consolidation,or tool use. Version 5 extends the outcome space from final answers to complete protected-effecttraces and explicitly models model identity, persistent memory, translation state, authorizationstate, and independently captured telemetry. New post-September-22 evidence includes aprovider-confirmed DNS path around an offline sandbox, provider-disclosed publication ofa secret token despite repeated human instructions, a demonstrated self-replicating promptinjectionmechanism confined to simulated tool calls, experimental evidence that local agents candelete their own traces, and new authorization research on provenance-bound memory, counterfactualpermission evaluation, and policy-constrained runtime validation. An integrity–behaviordecomposition and a history-uniform first-failure theorem separate behavioral reliability fromthe validity of enforcement and evidence boundaries. We add a trace-integrity bound, aversion-bound authorization model, and a state-transition rule that invalidates certificates afterunapproved model or interpreter mutation. Effect-preserving translation, policy automata,robust finite-state risk certificates, and pessimistic validation of incomplete traces provideexplicit proof obligations and counterexamples. Independent capability grants, out-of-bandenforcement, version-bound certificates, restricted teaching environments, and operationallyverified termination define a proposed architecture, not a claimed deployment achievement.Incident statements retain attribution and correction status; numerical fixtures are constructed,not empirical estimates. The contribution is a falsifiable account of expanding what humanscan verify without silently expanding what AI may do, not a universal safety guarantee orevidence of a superior AI metalanguage.

title: Local geographies of housing inequality: Neighbourhood trajectories of housing purchasing (un)affordability across neighbourhoods in England and Wales (2010-2023)
abstract: In recent decades, housing purchasing prices have outpaced incomes, increasing spatial inequalities and creating a growing challenge to homeownership. Despite housing markets being highly localised with most residential moves made at local scales, analyses of housing affordability have typically focused on national- and regional-level trends. We draw on a novel housing price dataset, to present the first neighbourhood-level analysis of housing (un)affordability trajectories across England and Wales (2010 to 2023). In doing so, we interrogate the reproduction of socio-spatial inequalities at the scale of everyday lives and raise questions about local geographies of housing inequality. We develop and map eight distinct neighbourhood trajectories of housing (un)affordability and reveal a nuanced geographical mosaic of housing (un)affordability across local areas. We show how different trajectories sit side-by-side, with localities of affordability in areas considered extremely unaffordable in aggregated analyses, such as London, and vice versa. While affordability pressures are experienced heterogeneously across the period, most neighbourhoods display a decline in affordability due to rising housing prices relative to incomes. Mapping these trajectories reveals a prominent spatial gradient in affordability pressures, which may narrow the ability of some residents to adjust to housing becoming less affordable, as surrounding areas are even less affordable. Overall, this geographically nuanced work illustrates unjust urban restructuring resulting from localised spatial manifestations of the financialisation of housing.
venue: Geoforum

title: On emotions and cooperative behavior for wildlife conservation
abstract: Abstract Emotions shape how people relate to wildlife, yet their role in encouraging cooperation for conservation has been largely overlooked in behavioral research. This study explores how emotional responses influence group decisions to support wildlife protection using an online experiment inspired by public goods games, an economic game often used to study cooperation in behavioral economics. A total of 246 participants, recruited via Amazon Mechanical Turk, were exposed to short video clips designed to trigger either positive or negative emotions. They were then asked to decide how much money to contribute to efforts aimed at conserving one of two species: the grey wolf ( Canis lupus ) or the wolverine ( Gulo gulo ). The results showed that emotions can influence willingness to cooperate, but their effects varied by species. Positive emotional states led to increased support for wolf conservation, while no clear effect was observed for the wolverine. Interestingly, when the same emotion was induced, financial contributions did not differ significantly between the two species. These findings suggest that emotional engagement, through positive messaging, may serve as an effective mechanism to promote cooperative behavior in wildlife conservation initiatives. However, the species-specific differences also highlight the importance of tailoring outreach and policy strategies to the emotional and cultural context surrounding each animal.
venue: European Journal of Wildlife Research

title: Multi-layer network analysis of deliberation in an online discussion platform: The case of Reddit
abstract: This paper proposes a novel multi-layer network model to study deliberation in online discussion platforms. The model comprises two layers: a discussion layer, which represents as a hierarchical tree the comment-to-comment replies within a given post, and an actor layer, which represents the actor-to-actor reply interactions. The interlayer links represent user-comment ownership. We use this network model to extend González-Bailón et al. (2010)’s foundational network analysis of argumentation and representation in discussion, by proposing two network metrics to measure the potential for deliberation in discussion threads. We also propose a new approach for identifying the boundaries that determine whether a given post is identified as deliberative, and for comparing the level of deliberation of collections of posts. We apply our new approach to a large Reddit dataset containing posts from 72 subreddits focused on different topics and demonstrate that our new metrics have construct validity in that observed differences in measured deliberation across categories of subreddits can be explained by the topics and purpose of the subreddits. While we find that some political subreddits exhibit high levels of deliberation thus indicating that online political talk can meet the prerequisites for deliberation, the level of deliberation in regional and sports subreddits was even higher. Analysis of the actor layer shows correlations between the deliberation measured on the discussion layer, and classical network metrics of the actor layer including degree distribution, assortativity, and the global clustering coefficient. These correlations reveal important insights into how the aggregate behaviour of users is related to deliberation.

title: FigBO: A Generalized Acquisition Function Framework with Look-Ahead Capability for Bayesian Optimization
abstract: Abstract Bayesian optimization is a powerful technique for optimizing expensive-to-evaluate black-box functions, consisting of two main components: a surrogate model and an acquisition function. In recent years, myopic acquisition functions have been widely adopted for their simplicity and effectiveness. However, their lack of look-ahead capability limits their performance. To address this limitation, we propose FigBO, a generalized acquisition function that incorporates the future impact of candidate points on global information gain. FigBO is a plug-and-play method that can integrate seamlessly with most existing myopic acquisition functions. Theoretically, we analyze the regret bound and convergence rate of FigBO when combined with the myopic base acquisition function expected improvement (EI), comparing them to those of standard EI. Empirically, extensive experimental results across diverse tasks demonstrate that FigBO achieves state-of-the-art performance and significantly faster convergence compared to existing methods.

title: Dollar Dominance in FX Trading
abstract: Over 85% of all foreign exchange (FX) transactions involve the U.S. dollar, whereas the United States accounts for a much smaller fraction of global economic activity. My paper attributes the dominance of the dollar in FX trading to strategic avoidance of price impact. Using a novel identification strategy, I show that, on average, 13% of the volume in dollar pairs arises from using the dollar as a vehicle currency to indirectly exchange two nondollar currencies. To rationalise this result, I derive three model-based conditions for dollar dominance. I empirically test these conditions and provide evidence consistent with the theoretical framework. This paper was accepted by Lukas Schmid, finance. Funding: F. Somogyi acknowledges financial support from the Swiss National Science Foundation (SNSF) [Grant 195095]. title: Self-esteem, Social Support, Personality and Psychological Well Being of Junior High School Student
abstract: The aims of this study was to understand how the relationship between self-esteem, social support, extraversion personality, agreeableness personality, conscientiousness personality, neuroticism personality, openness personality, and psychological well-being of the public junior high school stu- dents in Malang city. This study was a non-experimental study with correlational design. Results of this research showed a variable that has a relationship with the psychological well-being is self-esteem, social support, personality agreeableness, neuroticism personality and conscientiousness personality. Accumulated seventh influence of independent variables equal to 61% of the variance of psychological well-being can be explained by three independent variables, and the rest as many as 39% are caused by other factors.

title: Beyond AGI (Verification Intelligence series, Paper 8 of 12)
abstract: The artificial general intelligence research programme rests on an implicit equation: more capability produces more intelligence, and more intelligence produces better outcomes. This paper tests that equation against the evidence and finds it structurally unsound. The first link holds. Capability improvements do correspond to something that can reasonably be called intelligence — current frontier models reason with genuine sophistication across an extraordinary range of domains. The second link is broken. Enterprise failure rates, incident acceleration, and rework costs have remained stubbornly consistent through years of dramatic capability improvement. Intelligence does not produce better outcomes without verification infrastructure. This paper develops two arguments not made elsewhere in the series. The first is that capability and reliability are not merely uncorrelated but, in specific and consequential dimensions, inversely correlated — more capability actively produces less verifiability, less human oversight capacity, and greater potential for consequential undetected error. The inverse correlation operates through four identifiable channels (fluency, autonomy, confidence, and consequence), each of which intensifies as capability increases. The second is that the investment thesis underlying the AGI race — recursive capability gains producing superintelligence producing extraordinary value — has a structural flaw identical to the one that produced the 2008 financial crisis: recursive optimisation for internal metrics without verification against external reality. Others have recognised the verification gap from different angles: Anthropic's constitutional AI constrains model behaviour at training time; the EU AI Act mandates conformity assessment for high-risk systems; AVERI is building evaluation standards; Vitalik Buterin has proposed AI-assisted formal verification for code. Each addresses a real dimension of the problem. This paper examines the structural trajectory of the capability-only paradigm — the case that capability pursued as the sole objective produces a characteristic failure pattern in which systems become progressively more capable and progressively less trustworthy. The alternative paradigm — Verification Intelligence and Recursive General Intelligence — is described in the Verification Intelligence (Paper 4) and the Verification Substrate (Paper 5). This paper confines itself to the case against the current trajectory. ---
